planting.note: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Pink China taro thrives at a pond edge or in a large moisture-retentive container as much as in a border.

directions: Plant tubers after last frost, once soil has warmed, in rich, consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Pink China taro thrives at a pond edge or in a large moisture-retentive container as much as in a border. Large, matte, blue-green, heart-shaped leaves are carried on tall, distinctly pink-blushed petioles and stems, giving this taro selection a softer, more subtly colorful presence than the near-black or solid-green elephant ears more commonly grown. It brings bold, tropical foliage texture to a shaded bog garden, pond margin, or large container, tolerating standing water at the root zone as well as consistently moist ordinary garden soil. In zones colder than 8, lift and store tubers indoors over winter like dahlias, or grow the plant as a dramatic single-season annual.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; pink calla lily tolerates drier soil between waterings than white calla lily and is well suited to a large container.

directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; pink calla lily tolerates drier soil between waterings than white calla lily and is well suited to a large container. Narrow, dark green leaves speckled with translucent white spots set off elegant, funnel-shaped spathes in shades of soft pink to deep rose-red, smaller and more delicate than the familiar white calla lily but no less striking massed in a border or container. Native to summer-wet, winter-dry grasslands of South Africa, it goes dormant and can be left dry in the ground through a mild winter in zones 8-10, or lifted and stored like a dahlia tuber in colder climates. Plant in light shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch, and reduce watering as foliage yellows in fall to encourage the plant into its natural dormant period.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Greene's ginger lily is more shade-tolerant than most hardy gingers and its handsome burgundy-backed foliage benefits from protection from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Greene's ginger lily is more shade-tolerant than most hardy gingers and its handsome burgundy-backed foliage benefits from protection from hot afternoon sun. Broad, glossy leaves are washed deep maroon-purple on their undersides, and dense, upright spikes of brick-red to orange-red flowers rise above the foliage in late summer, standing out both for their unusual true-red color, rare among hardy gingers, and for the ornamental foliage that provides interest even between bloom cycles. Native to the eastern Himalayas, it tolerates more shade than most Hedychium species, making it a good choice for a shaded tropical-style border where sun-loving ginger lilies would struggle to flower well. Mulch heavily over winter in zone 8 to protect the dormant rhizomes from hard freezes.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; spiked ginger lily is among the more cold-hardy Hedychium species, tolerating brief freezes once its rhizomes are established and mulched.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; spiked ginger lily is among the more cold-hardy Hedychium species, tolerating brief freezes once its rhizomes are established and mulched. Broad, banana-like leaves rise from stout canes topped in late summer by dense, upright spikes of fragrant, pale yellow to cream flowers with a prominent orange-red throat marking, followed by showy orange seed capsules that split to reveal bright red seeds persisting into fall. Native to Himalayan forests from Afghanistan to southwestern China, its aromatic rhizome has long been used in traditional medicine and incense in its native range, and the plant itself brings both fragrance and bold tropical texture to a shaded or partly sunny border. Mulch heavily over winter at the colder end of its range and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ermine canna's compact size suits it to container culture and smaller borders where full-sized cannas would overwhelm the space.

directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ermine canna's compact size suits it to container culture and smaller borders where full-sized cannas would overwhelm the space. A long-cultivated dwarf canna selection, it produces clean, fresh green foliage and clusters of creamy white flowers held well above the leaves from summer through fall, offering a softer, more subtle color option than the bright reds, oranges, and yellows typical of most cannas. Its compact habit makes it a good choice for the middle of a mixed border, a large container, or the edge of a pond planting where taller cannas would need to be set further back. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring, and mulch heavily or lift rhizomes for winter storage outside zones 8-11.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Stingray alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Stingray alocasia is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen moved indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. This distinctive hybrid produces long, narrow, undulating leaf blades that taper to a slender, whip-like drip tip, giving each leaf a striking silhouette reminiscent of a stingray's body and tail unlike the broad, arrow-shaped leaves of most other alocasias. Its unusual leaf form makes it a conversation-piece specimen for a shaded patio container or the protected understory of a tropical-themed border, where high humidity and consistent moisture keep the foliage looking its best. Protect from direct hot sun, which scorches the leaves, and from cold below the mid-50s Fahrenheit, which causes the plant to go dormant or suffer dieback.

planting.note: Plant rooted stem cuttings or divisions after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; fiery costus is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Plant rooted stem cuttings or divisions after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; fiery costus is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Fleshy, spirally arranged leaves wind distinctively up thick, jointed stems in the characteristic 'spiral ginger' habit, with small yellow-orange flowers emerging from cone-like bracts at the stem tips through the warm season. Native to Mexico and Central America, its fresh leaves are chewed or brewed as a folk remedy for blood sugar management in traditional Latin American and South Asian herbal medicine, earning it the common name insulin plant, though this use has not been established by rigorous clinical evidence and it should not replace medical treatment. Grown primarily for its striking spiraled foliage in a humid, shaded container or greenhouse setting, it propagates readily from stem cuttings rooted in water or moist soil.
